Lead story

Ray: Okay, so here's the problem. When a system changes phase, like ice melting, there are two broad flavors. A first-order transition is abrupt, with two phases coexisting. A continuous one is smoother, and right at the critical point you get power-law scaling.

Ada: And the catch is that a weak first-order transition can look continuous.

Ray: Exactly. The paper says weak first-order transitions can show long stretches of pseudocritical scaling that mimic genuine criticality. The test case is the dilute Baxter Wu model, whose apparent criticality has been debated for a long time.

Ada: So what did the authors actually do?

Ray: They combined two tools. One is conformal perturbation theory, which describes small nudges away from a critical theory. The other is symmetry-resolved tensor-network level spectroscopy, which means numerically computing the energy levels of the system using tensor networks and sorting them by symmetry. With those, they wrote down a slowly running coupling in a form they could handle numerically, and built a general, flow-based diagnostic.

Ada: Running coupling meaning the strength of an interaction changes as you zoom out.

Ray: Right. And the key result is that the apparent criticality comes from a marginally relevant renormalization group flow. Marginally relevant means the coupling grows, but very slowly. Eventually it drives the system into a first-order regime with phase coexistence. They also report that the flows for the dilute and self-dual Baxter Wu models collapse onto the multicritical phase diagram of the dilute four-state Potts model.

Ada: Okay, referee hat on. Is this an experiment or a simulation?

Ray: It's theory plus numerics on a model. The abstract doesn't describe a lab material.

Ada: Does it scale? What lattice sizes, what error bars?

Ray: The abstract doesn't say. No sizes or numbers are given there.

Ada: Fair. So why should anyone care?

Ray: Because the caution is general. Power-law-looking scaling in finite-size data doesn't prove a continuous transition. That's the blurb's reading, and the diagnostic is meant to be generic, so others can check their own cases.

Baxter–Wu 'criticality' is really a marginal flow to first order

arXiv · spin models & criticality · 8/10

The abstract reports that the long-debated apparent criticality of the dilute Baxter–Wu model comes from a marginally relevant renormalization-group flow that ends in first-order coexistence. The authors used conformal perturbation theory and tensor-network level spectroscopy. It is a general caution: power-law-looking scaling in finite-size data can mimic a continuous phase transition.

Kinetomagnetism linked to altermagnetism through symmetry classification

Physical Review Materials · 8/10

The abstract reports that broken parity-time symmetry is both necessary and sufficient for kinetomagnetism, and that all altermagnets can show it. The framework is said to unify piezomagnetism, nonlinear Hall responses and spin-splitting torques. It is a symmetry classification rather than a materials prediction, and the abstract says nothing about anisotropy.

Ten-loop RG gives O(N) exponents; N=1 matches the bootstrap

arXiv · spin models & criticality · 7/10

The paper extends the fixed-dimension renormalization-group functions of the 3D O(N) model to ten loops, using GPU-based Monte Carlo integration. The resummed N=1 values, ν=0.62997(51) and η=0.0333(18), are reported alongside conformal-bootstrap values, with deviations growing at N=3. These serve as reference exponents for checking simulation output, though their precision is lower than the bootstrap's.

Diffusion models sample the 2D classical Heisenberg model

arXiv · statistical mechanics · 8/10

A score-based diffusion model is trained on the two-dimensional O(3) lattice model, and the authors report that multiscale coarse-graining modestly improves accuracy and cost over direct sampling. They add Schwinger-Dyson diagnostics for two-point correlations that do not require reverse diffusion. It is a generative alternative to standard Monte Carlo sampling, with only 2D and modest gains claimed, so its behavior near the critical point is worth watching.

TmZnGaO4 shows easy-c-axis anisotropy and a one-third plateau

Physical Review Materials · 7/10

The abstract reports a new triangular-lattice antiferromagnet with strong easy-c-axis anisotropy in magnetization curves, a one-third magnetization plateau, and no long-range order. Broad specific-heat anomalies appear at 0.11 K and 2.81 K. The magnetic ion is non-Kramers thulium rather than cerium, but the study is a clear example of how directional single-crystal measurements reveal magnetic behavior.

Mechanical squeeze reportedly changes altermagnet magnetism

ScienceDaily · Materials · 6/10

A ScienceDaily summary says strain dramatically alters the magnetic and electrical properties of altermagnets. The summary gives no numbers, so the size of the effect is unknown. The original paper would be needed for anisotropy or ordering-temperature data.

Physics-guided CNN infers DMI and disorder from domain images

J. Magnetism & Magnetic Materials · 6/10

No abstract is available, so the details are unconfirmed. The title suggests a data-efficient machine-learning method for extracting magnetic parameters such as the Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya interaction (DMI) and disorder from magnetic domain images. Whether it was trained on simulated or measured images is not stated.

Evolutionary search builds interpretable spatial descriptors

arXiv · ML materials discovery · 6/10

The abstract reports a genetic algorithm that optimizes spatial partitions and pooling choices, uses SHAP maps to attribute importance, and trades prediction error against descriptor size. It was demonstrated on local spectra and hysteresis loops. Applying it to other kinds of structural data would be an extension; that is my inference, since the demonstrations are on microscopy-type data.

The article says the new generation replaces off-the-shelf parts with a custom architecture built for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) integration. EvSLAM benchmarks event cameras under aggressive 6-DoF motion

The abstract reports an analysis of event-based visual odometry and visual-inertial methods, flags shortcomings in public datasets, and introduces a new benchmark framework for six-degree-of-freedom motion. It is aimed at robotics rather than melt pools. Its useful contribution is how it handles evaluation limits for event data.

Particle inertia linked to large pores in powder-blown DED

J. Manufacturing Processes · 5/10

No abstract is available, so the details are unconfirmed. The title links particle inertia to the formation of large pores and to material-dependent melt-pool response. This is powder-blown directed energy deposition rather than laser powder bed fusion, so whether the mechanism carries over is unclear.

Theoretical Physics

Mg doping cuts Ising-like Co chains into finite segments

arXiv · spin models & criticality · 7/10

In Ba(Co,Mg)2V2O8, nonmagnetic magnesium breaks Ising-like antiferromagnetic chains into short pieces. Neutron scattering and numerical work find spinons confined at the chain ends, along with a cluster mode in which a whole Néel-ordered segment flips together. It is a real-crystal example of finite-size physics.

Long-range transverse-field Ising chain: exponents near the crossover

arXiv · spin models & criticality · 6/10

The paper proposes a weakly coupled description near the crossover to short-range behavior and predicts the dynamical exponent z. The prediction is checked with DMRG, a numerical method for quantum many-body systems, on chains up to 128 sites. It concerns a model rather than any specific material.

Can a gapped quantum phase become gapless under tiny perturbations?

arXiv · quantum physics · 6/10

Physicists usually assume that a system with an energy gap stays gapped under weak nudges. The authors show this can fail: there are gapped local Hamiltonians that become gapless under an arbitrarily weak perturbation. In one dimension, such cases must be fine-tuned and break translation invariance. This bears on how robust a quantum phase really is, which underlies phase diagrams.

Quanta: gravity seems holographic, but what does it mean?

Quanta Magazine · Physics · 6/10

Holography is the finding that a gravitational theory in some space can be equivalent to a theory without gravity living on that space's lower-dimensional boundary, so gravity can effectively collapse a dimension. Quanta reports that physicists do not yet understand what this implies about reality. It is a good overview of the big-picture debate in quantum gravity.
